newsitem.title: USA: Away on business: service, please.
newsitem.headline: Away on business: service, please.

text.p: A reader writes: "I am a black, female business traveller. Occasionally I sense that flight attendants may not serve me in the proper order. That is, regardless of my seat assignment, I am served last.
"Is there a certain order in which passengers should be served? For instance, from the window to the aisle, or vice-versa?"

We asked the Association of Flight Attendants, which said that while there appear to be no rules, and while training may differ among the carriers, the most practical method for handing out drinks and meals is to work from the passenger farthest from the attendant to the one nearest.
In a one-aisle plane with three seats on each side, such as a Boeing 737 or Airbus 320, that would mean the window seats get served first, the aisle seats last.

If someone on the aisle is served first, the attendant would have to lean over that food or drink to reach the middle or window seat -- or an interior seat on in the middle section of a wide-body plane.

"It's quicker and easier to do it that way," a spokeswoman said after taking an informal poll among former flight attendants. "It's something that may have grown out of common sense and improvisation."

But on any given flight, depending on how crowded it is and how busy the attendants are, there could be variations. Typical short-haul flights where food service is offered usually involve only a small snack that can be handed out in any order and drink service is a beat-the-clock affair.

Regarding the racial part of the question, most recent flights we've been on were so crowded the attendants did not seem to have had a chance to think about slights, which in any case would seem to run counter to the customer-first attitude cabin attendants usually seem to manage.
More evidence of crowding in the skies comes in the July edition of Consumer Reports Travel Letter, which offers its annual guide to airline seat comfort.
It reports that airline load factors -- which measure seat occupancy -- are averaging 85 percent, up sharply from what they were when the publication did its last report a year ago.

And because published load factors don't count travelers flying free on frequent flier coupons or airline employes, the actual occupancy of flights is higher, it said, with the most heavily loaded flights -- those approaching 100 percent -- carrying more than half of all passengers.
The publication's report breaks information down by airline, showing how each carrier configures aircraft interiors and resulting comfort levels.

The Boeing 777 as configured by United took the top comfort score for coach-economy seats, though the publication advises against sitting in rows 16, 31, 40 or 43 of United's 777 because those rows have narrower seats.
Information about the Travel Letter can be obtained by calling 1 800 234-1970.

Business travelers: question, complaint or pet peeve? Write Away on Business, c/o Reuters, Room 1170, 311 S. Wacker Dr., Chicago 60606. Or e-mail Mike.Conlon(at)Reuters.com. We cannot promise personal replies but will try to address letters as space permits.
